item.title: An Ancient Wall Sheds Light On an Old Question: Where Did Paris Begin?
item.description:
An ancient wall, discovered recently during excavations to shore up a hospital in Paris, could help clarify the location of the city’s original settlements around the time that Julius Caesar chronicled the Roman conquest of Gaul, according to experts.

The stone and wood wall, which measures 72 feet, is characteristic of Gallic fortifications dating from the late Iron Age, which ended around the first century B.C. The structure was found this summer, along with a Gallic spearhead, at a construction site inside the hospital Hôtel Dieu, on the Île de la Cité, an island on the Seine River in the heart of Paris.

The French culture minister, Catherine Pégard, described it in a statement on Wednesday as “one of the most important archaeological remains ever discovered for understanding Gallic Lutetia.”

Lutetia, the Latin name for the city that would eventually become Paris, was built by a Gallic tribe that lived along the Seine River probably as early as the fourth century B.C. Julius Caesar, in his chronicle of the Gallic Wars — the Roman campaigns fought between 58 and 50 B.C. against tribes in Gaul — described Lutetia as a fortification built on an island in the Seine. Rome conquered the city in 52 B.C.

In his account, Caesar describes Roman legions moving “for Lutetia, a town of the Parisii, situated on an island in the river Seine.” He adds that Gallic tribes, learning of the Roman advance, had “ordered Lutetia to be set on fire and the bridges belonging to the town to be cut down.”

Until now, Caesar’s vague description and the lack of archaeological evidence made the location of a Gallic city on the Seine a source of debate among French scholars. Many questioned whether Lutetia was located in the heart of Paris or somewhere else. Some argued that the settlement was actually in Nanterre, a suburb west of Paris, citing archaeological discoveries there in the 1990s.

“I was among the colleagues who wrote that Lutetia was probably not located on the Île de la Cité, since at the time — in the 1990s — the evidence was really very, very scant,” said Matthieu Poux, an archaeology professor at the University of Lyon II.

But the finding of the wall had changed his mind, Mr. Poux said, adding that he now had no doubt that the location of the ancient city was on the Île de la Cité.

While Ms. Pégard, the culture minister, said further scientific research was needed to verify the wall’s “function and its chronology,” initial carbon dating of wood fragments indicates that the wall dates back to between 200 B.C. and 10 B.C., which matches the period chronicled by Julius Caesar.

Moreover, the wall bears traces of a fire, potentially in keeping with Caesar’s account. “Charred seeds and the remains of a burned wooden building were also unearthed,” the culture ministry said, which may correspond to Caesar’s account that the Gauls set fire to their settlement before fleeing the advancing Romans.

Archaeological finds have shed significant light on the development of Roman-era Lutetia. Roman artifacts have been found under what is today the Latin Quarter, and a Roman residential area was uncovered under the Luxembourg Gardens, roughly a mile south of the Île de la Cité.

Much less was known about Gallic Lutetia. But, as Mr. Poux said, this discovery under the hospital “increases the amount of data available on this topic tenfold in a single excavation campaign.”

The finding, he said, could be a “starting point” for other archaeological discoveries on the Île de la Cité, though he noted that digs are limited to ongoing refurbishment of buildings, slowing the progress.

The culture ministry said further excavations would take place in the vicinity of the site, and that the entire wall would ultimately be moved to be studied and displayed. Emmanuel Grégoire, the mayor of Paris, said the city would “share this heritage with the people of Paris and all of those who cherish the city.”

item.title: India’s Election Panel Faces New Scrutiny Over Voter Roll Revisions
item.description:
India’s election commission rushed through measures that could exclude tens of millions of people from voting, even as two of the three commissioners raised concerns over the legality of the moves, according to an explosive investigation published in a major Indian newspaper on Wednesday.

The investigation, by The Indian Express, is intensifying concerns about election integrity that have rattled India over the past year.

The report, which drew from internal documents and interviews, found that the two commissioners questioned the legality of several aspects of an effort to revise India’s voter rolls and officially recorded their opposition. But the decisions were nonetheless made unilaterally by Gyanesh Kumar, the lead commissioner. The election commission, which oversees all elections in India, is required by law to make its decisions by a majority.

Opposition parties have often accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi of using his influence over the voting process to entrench the power of his Bharatiya Janata Party, but this report is the first indication of serious objections raised from within India’s election system.

In a statement, the election commission said that The Indian Express drew on “differing views and deliberations” between the three commissioners rather than official statements of protest. The statement was signed by a junior official, not the commissioners, and did not explicitly deny that two of the commissioners had recorded their opposition to certain moves.

Sambit Patra, a spokesman for Mr. Modi’s party, told reporters that the commission’s decisions were made “with unanimity” and that any earlier deliberation was “a sign of a healthy democracy.”

The election commission did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the details in the Indian Express report.

The newspaper’s investigation focused on an exercise called the Special Intensive Revision, which began last year and was billed as an effort to clean up the electoral rolls across the world’s largest democracy, but it faced serious challenges from the outset.

The process, which is not yet complete, has been chaotic, burdening some of the country’s poorest citizens with document requirements that are often contradictory. In Bihar, the first state subject to the exercise, local officials managing it often admitted — including to reporters from The New York Times — that they were so overwhelmed with the enormity of the task against a tight deadline that they struggled to ensure the fairness of the rolls.

The revision process has resulted in the deletion of tens of millions of names from voter rolls, including in several states that have gone to the polls to elect their local governments amid confusion and chaos. Some regions could face a reduction of as much as 30 percent of their electoral rolls, according to election commission data.

While there is so far no clear data drawing a link between voter deletions and the performance of Mr. Modi’s party in recent elections, election analysts have said that the scale of confusion and chaos has only added to the opposition parties’ disadvantage.

The revision process involved several decisions by the commission, including the addition of a stringent step to the registration of new voters, despite two of the commissioners’ deeming it “unauthorized and illegal,” according to The Indian Express. The newspaper also noted that access to electoral rolls has become increasingly centralized, and that many local officials complained about not having proper access to those databases, making it difficult to add legitimate names.

Ahead of a bitterly fought election in the state of West Bengal earlier this year, in which Mr. Modi’s party unseated the incumbent, the revisions resulted in millions of people being deleted from voter rolls. Judicial officers stepped in at the last minute and ruled to restore 1.5 million voters who appealed their deletion, but the election commission blocked the restoration of those voters.

However, the investigation quoted from documents showing that two of the three commissioners were unaware who was lodging the legal appeals by the commission to block those voters from the rolls.

After the investigation was published, opposition parties were quick to call for action.

Leaders of the Indian National Congress, the main opposition, described Mr. Kumar as “bulldozing his own organization, and hijacking his own colleagues” and called on him to resign “out of shame.” The Aam Admi Party, another opposition party, called for his arrest and prosecution.

O.P. Rawat, a former election commissioner of India, said the allegations are “very serious,” but needed to be verified through an official inquiry.

“If it is proved after inquiry, then it is a very serious setback. It is unprecedented. It has never happened in the history of the Election Commission of India,” he said.

Mr. Rawat said that the revision exercise faced credible questions. In West Bengal, he noted, the tribunals used to appeal voter roll deletions have found that an overwhelming majority of the voters removed were actually eligible voters.

“They could not cast their votes,” Mr. Rawat said. “That is the most serious issue so far at the doors of the election commission.”

item.title: Trump’s New Favorite Neighbor: Mexico
item.description:
The U.S.-Canada relationship has imploded. But along the other, typically more contentious U.S. border, a partnership is blooming.

In his second term, President Trump has made Mexico — once his favorite punching bag — now one of his closest and most important allies.

The two nations have expanded cooperation to slow illegal border crossings to historic lows, joined forces to disrupt drug cartels and increased commerce to become each other’s biggest trading partners.

Mr. Trump opened his second term by threatening airstrikes in Mexico to stop immigration and drug trafficking at the border. But after a year of tensions, the relationship is lifting off as U.S. relations with Canada have nose-dived.

Trump administration officials have recently begun praising Mexican efforts against the cartels, including in an official declaration last week, though they say they still want more action. Military and security agencies on both sides of the border have significantly deepened their ties, with officials in both countries saying there has never been better collaboration. And U.S. officials have effectively shelved plans for U.S. airstrikes on Mexican soil, at least for now, according to one U.S. official, one former Pentagon official and two Mexican officials.

Now, the Trump administration also appears to be nearing a trade agreement directly with Mexico.

Last week, President Claudia Sheinbaum of Mexico said she and Mr. Trump had reached agreements on several trade issues in a long phone call. Hours after that call, Mr. Trump said at a campaign rally that the two nations were “very close” to a trade deal.

Roberto Lazzeri, Mexico’s ambassador in Washington, said in an interview that he hoped they would have some sort of deal by the U.S. midterm elections. “We’re on a good track,” he said.

It is a twist few expected when Mr. Trump returned to office: Mexico, not Canada, as his chosen neighbor. The shift reflects how he has shuffled the global map, particularly in favor of countries willing to cooperate with his demands.

For this article, Times reporters interviewed nearly a dozen U.S. and Mexican officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations.

In his address to the United Nations on Tuesday, Mr. Trump said he was focused on getting Latin American nations to help fight against drug traffickers. “I’m very proud to tell you we have a very good relationship with the Mexican government,” he said. “We’ve made great strides, very great strides with Mexico.”

His transactional approach on the world stage also comes with unpredictability. While he has repeatedly complimented Ms. Sheinbaum as a world leader he respects, he also posted an image this month of the American flag superimposed over her nation.

But Mexico is also critical to the success of the Trump agenda. He campaigned on stopping the flow of migrants and fentanyl across the border, and the U.S. economy relies in part on Mexico, especially amid the trade war with the other top U.S. trading partner, Canada.

In the face of Mr. Trump’s threats of airstrikes, ground troops and tariffs, Ms. Sheinbaum has focused on his priorities. She stationed 10,000 troops along Mexico’s side of the border and ramped up operations against cartels, often using U.S. intelligence.

From the final full month of the Biden administration to last month, total monthly border encounters — which count both arrests between crossings and migrants turned away at official ports — fell 87 percent, to 12,200.

Fentanyl seizures at the U.S.-Mexico border dropped by half in the first half of this year, compared with the same period in 2024. And the Sheinbaum administration has already destroyed 2,700 drug labs in two years, 100 more than the preceding government destroyed in six.

The Sheinbaum government has taken a much more aggressive approach against the cartels, adding more than 600 new investigative agents, compared with zero under her predecessor, according to a Mexican official.

Its work has been augmented by deeper collaboration with the United States.

Since last year, U.S. security agencies have added hundreds of new Mexican law enforcement officials to Mexico’s so-called vetted units, which are specialized task forces that have been trained and vetted by U.S. authorities and which receive U.S. intelligence on cartel targets, according to Mexican and U.S. officials.

The Mexican Navy also now interdicts nearly every boat in Mexican waters that U.S. intelligence flags as carrying drug traffickers, Mexican and U.S. officials said.

U.S. officials still want more. The State Department said in a statement: “The Mexicans have done more than they ever have before to address these challenges, but it is still not nearly enough — they know that, we’ve expressed that to them.”

Mexico and the United States are also doing more business together. In the first half of the year, total trade of goods between the countries increased about 14 percent compared with a year prior, to nearly half a trillion dollars.

Mexico, which now accounts for roughly one-sixth of all trade for the United States, has effectively had the lowest tariff rate of any major trading partner. A new trade agreement could lower that even further. At the same time, Mexico has imposed up to 50 percent tariffs on many Chinese imports, thrilling U.S. officials.

The expanding partnership has been fostered in part by a warm relationship between Mr. Trump and Ms. Sheinbaum, developed over more than 20 conversations.

Ms. Sheinbaum speaks English on their calls and aims to clearly explain Mexico’s achievements in advancing Mr. Trump’s priorities, including by sending charts that show declining border crossings and fentanyl seizures, according to two people with direct knowledge of the calls.

She is firm but coolheaded while telling Mr. Trump that Mexico would not accept direct U.S. intervention on Mexican soil, these people said. She has also recently brought up the U.S. government’s poor treatment of some Mexican migrants, arguing they are hard-working people who contribute to the U.S. economy, they said.

Mr. Trump and his advisers continually push for more action against undocumented migrants and drug traffickers, but he is also warm toward his Mexican counterpart, they said. He has repeatedly called Ms. Sheinbaum elegant and said she has a “beautiful voice,” both in public and on calls with her, according to three officials.

After Mr. Trump told reporters this month that he could cut trade ties with Mexico if he wished, he added: “I don’t want to do that, because I get along very well with the president. We like the president. We respect her a lot.”

The moment’s good vibes are exceptional when considering the tensions just a few months ago.

Two C.I.A. officers died in an April car crash during a drug lab operation in Chihuahua state. The incident infuriated Ms. Sheinbaum, who said her cabinet was unaware of U.S. activities in the state. Then U.S. prosecutors indicted a sitting Mexican governor from Ms. Sheinbaum’s party, accusing him of aiding cartels.

Ms. Sheinbaum walked a delicate line in response. She refused to order the indicted governor’s arrest, but privately pressured him to step down. She warned of U.S. threats against Mexican sovereignty while continuing to expand security cooperation. Over time, the tensions defused.

Mexican officials say her composed approach is the opposite of Canada’s tack — and it is working.

“We have learned that taking a belligerent or isolationist attitude is not going to achieve anything; it’s going to drive up prices and products,” said Ricardo Monreal, a Mexican lawmaker who leads Ms. Sheinbaum’s coalition in Congress.

“Sheinbaum has gotten it right: not taking the bait,” he added. “Mexico is not positioned for a major confrontation, and I think the president understands that very well, unlike Canada.”

For instance, when Mr. Trump posted the image of the U.S. flag over Mexico, Ms. Sheinbaum posted from her own account that Mexico will always remain independent, but did not directly address his post.

Mr. Lazzeri, Mexico’s ambassador in Washington, said in an interview that Mexican officials don’t take such posts too seriously. “It’s a picture, not an official statement. So I wouldn’t know how to react to a picture,” he said.

When asked if it was currently the best moment in U.S.-Mexico relations, Mr. Lazzeri called it a moment of “the deepest coordination.”

“The best moment is very subjective,” he added, “as the world is going through a complex moment.”

Yet there is a wing of Ms. Sheinbaum’s political party, Morena, that wants her to push back harder.

Washington’s revocation of visas of Morena political figures, including the son of Ms. Sheinbaum’s predecessor, former President Andrés Manuel Lopez Obrador, has particularly angered some who accuse the Trump administration of trying to destabilize their leftist movement. Mexico is one of the last Latin American countries still run by a leftist, after a streak of seven consecutive right-wing election victories in the region since Mr. Trump took office.

“It’s part of a broader campaign to discredit and harass our movement,” said Gerardo Fernández Noroña, a Morena senator. “We’re under attack, facing terrible interference from the U.S. government.”

In Ms. Sheinbaum’s daily news conference, that thinking sometimes shines through. She frequently warns of U.S. influence in her country. And when the two nations’ deepening relationship comes up, she frames it with a new favorite motto: “coordination without subordination.”

Eric Schmitt and Tyler Pager contributed reporting from Washington, and Steve Fisher and Maria Abi-Habib from Mexico City.

item.title: Tigray Region Mobilizes Forces Against Ethiopian Central Government
item.description:
The authorities in Ethiopia’s Tigray region said on Wednesday that they had mobilized their forces against the federal government, signaling a severe escalation in a conflict that analysts fear will lead to another all-out war.

Tigrayan forces seized the airport in the city of Mekelle early on Wednesday as well as others in the northern region, displacing federal forces in a direct challenge to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s central government.

Tigray’s regional administration accused the federal government on Wednesday of starting an invasion, pointing to a series of recent attacks, including an assault by infantry, drones and artillery.

Tigray, which borders Eritrea and is inhabited mostly by the Tigrayan ethnic group, has played a crucial role in contemporary Ethiopian politics. Its forces led a coalition that overthrew a military regime in 1991. Then its leader, Meles Zenawi, ruled the country until his death in 2012, undertaking significant reforms. During that time, Ethiopia became one of Africa’s fastest growing economies.

But hundreds of thousands of people were killed in a two-year war between the central government and Tigrayan forces that began in 2020 and drew in Eritrea on the side of Mr. Abiy, who had taken power in 2018. That conflict led to mass starvation and accusations of sexual violence.

Since then, rivalries between powers in the Persian Gulf have further unsettled the Horn of Africa, raising concerns that another conflict in Ethiopia, the second most populous country in Africa, could transform into a large-scale regional war.

“Our army, the shield for the existence and safety of its people, has been instructed to counter the attack and genocidal invasion and has entered defense operations,” Tigray’s regional administration said in a statement on Wednesday. “We call upon our army, all our people and allies in our struggle to consolidate their unity and strengthen their fight.”

The loss of the airports — critical for military advantage — was confirmed by an adviser to Mr. Abiy, Getachew Reda.

The Tigray People’s Liberation Front also launched an offensive against government positions in the northern regions of Afar and Amhara, according to Mr. Getachaw, writing on social media.

“The T.P.L.F. politico-military leadership has obviously taken irresponsibility to new heights,” he said.

The rapid military developments follow months in which the two sides have appeared near the brink of conflict without tipping over into it. Tigray has conscripted recruits into its forces and taken control of the region’s parliament.

Over the weekend, it joined a new alliance of seven rebel groups in different parts of the country, saying they would overthrow Mr. Abiy’s government and replace it with an inclusive democracy.

The U.S. ambassador to Ethiopia, Ervin Massinga, noted that the United States had imposed sanctions on the leadership of the T.P.L.F. earlier this year. He criticized what he said was Tigray’s “poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive” and said dialogue was still possible.

One open question is the role that Eritrea and its leader, Isaias Afwerki, would play in any hostilities.

Eritrea and Ethiopia were hostile neighbors for decades until, until 2018, then joined forces in fighting in Tigray from 2020 to 2022. But since that war ended, relations between Tigrayan leaders and Mr. Isaias have warmed.

Mr. Abiy has talked recently of wanting a port on the Red Sea to facilitate trade and expand its security presence, given that Ethiopia is landlocked. Eritrea’s military would resist any Ethiopian attempt to seize its port of Assab.

This week’s events suggested the potential start of a new, full-scale war, according to experts, but it was unclear how the government in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, would respond and de-escalation, potentially through mediation, appeared possible.

“It looks like the declaration of full-fledged war,” said Mehari Taddele Maru of the European University Institute in Florence, who served as the African Union’s Migration program director in the late 2000s. “Everyone is preparing the ground for what is to come.”

A spokeswoman for Mr. Abiy did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
